effect_mechanism: A Swedish modelling study puts the opportunity cost of riparian buffers, the net present value of forgone forestry, at 3300 to 3500 USD per hectare of productive forest; per hectare of total forestland, 1800–2300 USD for hydrologically adapted buffers against 2700–2900 USD for fixed-width buffers; and 3400 USD per hectare on average for hydrologically adapted buffers [ev_project_cost_tiwari16_2, ev_project_cost_tiwari16_3, ev_project_cost_tiwari16_4, ev_project_cost_tiwari16_5].
conditionality: No class is stated: these are modelled opportunity costs of retaining trees in production forest, not restoration expenditures, from a single modelling study in a high-income boreal catchment outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_project_cost_tiwari16_2, ev_project_cost_tiwari16_5]. The figures count different areas (productive forest versus total forestland), so they do not pool into one range [ev_project_cost_tiwari16_2, ev_project_cost_tiwari16_3, ev_project_cost_tiwari16_4]. A second independent source, or a measured restoration cost, is what is missing.

effect_mechanism: Modelling in Sweden finds that wider buffers cost more, that adding groundwater-discharge hotspots raised protection at a small cost, and that retaining trees in low-productivity stands minimises buffer cost; the same paper reports second-hand a US study in which a site-specific variable-width buffer was more cost-effective than a fixed-width one [ev_project_cost_tiwari16_6, ev_project_cost_tiwari16_7, ev_project_cost_tiwari16_8, ev_project_cost_tiwari16_9].
conditionality: No class is stated: these are relative design statements with no amount and no control, from a single paper (its own model plus a second-hand citation), and the width statement is a cost increase rather than a reduction [ev_project_cost_tiwari16_6, ev_project_cost_tiwari16_9]. Both settings are high-income and outside the LIC/LMIC target. A second independent source or a measured cost comparison is what is missing.
